# B3. Other parameters {#oecd-parameters}

## The U.S. across the intertemporal and the Frisch elasticity {#oecd-frisch}

The figure shows the counterfactuals of section {{< var p.sec_oecd >}} on the U.S. across the two elasticities that
govern the households' responses. The intertemporal elasticity ρ varies at the paper's Frisch elasticity; the Frisch
elasticity ξ varies under log preferences. At each ξ the U.S. and France are recalibrated to the same targets, so the
discount factor, the political weight of the old and the taste for leisure take new values. The ranking of the
determinants holds at every ξ of the grid: ageing and the design move the tax rate most, France's characteristics
far less. A higher Frisch elasticity dampens the responses of the tax rate a little and some responses of savings by more,
and it enlarges the responses of hours, since labor supply is more elastic, all but that to France's taste for
leisure, which it makes a little smaller.

::: {.oa-explorer}
{{< include _generated/exhibits/OECD_Frisch-head.qmd >}}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {counterfactuals, control, ROWS_GIVEN, RHO, XI, GIVEN_OUTCOMES} from "./assets/oa.js"
oecd = FileAttachment("_generated/data/OECD_Counterfactuals.csv").csv({typed: true})
viewof b3Across = control("radio", [["the intertemporal elasticity ρ", "rho"], ["the Frisch elasticity ξ", "xi"]],
                          {key: "across", label: "Compare across", value: "rho"})
viewof b3Out = control("radio", GIVEN_OUTCOMES, {key: "outcome", label: "Outcome", value: "tau"})
counterfactuals(oecd.filter(d => d.host === "US" && d.calibration === "commonX" && d.effect === "full"
                                 && d.source === (b3Across === "rho" ? "main" : "xi")),
  {rows: ROWS_GIVEN, series: b3Across === "rho" ? RHO : XI, outcome: b3Out, width,
   facets: [{label: b3Across === "rho" ? "U.S., ξ = 0.3" : "U.S., ρ = 1", filter: d => true}]})
```

## The tax rate and inherited savings {#oecd-state}

The tax rate of the Markov equilibrium is a function of the state the economy inherits, the savings of the previous
period's young. The figure shows the U.S. tax policy of 2020 at inherited savings below and above their value on the
equilibrium path, each IES at its own calibration. Under log preferences the tax rate does not depend on the state
(section {{< var p.sec_LOG >}}). Away from log preferences it does: at an IES of one half the tax rate falls as
inherited savings rise, and at an IES of two it rises, less steeply.

{{< include _generated/exhibits/US_TaxState.qmd >}}

Because the tax rate depends on the state, the 2020 electorate's choice reaches the 2050 tax rate through the
savings it leaves: a higher tax lowers what the young save, and the 2050 electorate's policy responds to those
savings. Voters in the Markov equilibrium take this into account. The table gives the size of that strategic term at
the equilibrium path, the elasticity of savings to the tax times the slope of the 2050 policy function. It is small
at both values of the IES. At one half, a higher tax in 2020 raises the 2050 tax by a small fraction of a percentage
point per point, since the policy falls with savings; at two, it lowers it, by less.
